docs.text: Physical Interaction Design ("Gesture Capture") The Physical Interaction Design course is offered as part of the Digicrea and CCNT master's programs at Université Jean Monnet in Saint-Étienne (France). Its goal is to provide an overview of embedded electronics in the context of the arts. A wide variety of topics are covered: basic electronics, sensor technologies, microcontroller programming, embedded audio, and digital fabrication. By the end of the course, students will be able to design their own control interfaces as well as interactive installations. More specifically, the following topics are covered: Digital luthery and DMIs (Digital Musical Instruments); Microcontroller programming (e.g., Arduino); Basic electronics; Digital fabrication fundamentals; Use of sensors; Controller creation; Camera-based gesture capture; Basics of embedded audio; Use of AI in the of gesuture capture and NIME. A project in which students will create their own physical controller will serve as the course assessment. Instructor Romain Michon ( romain.michon@univ-st-etienne.fr ). Feel free to reach out to him at any point during the semester. Schedule and Course Materials All the course material is available on this website. Lectures can be found in the lectures tab in the above menu. Assignments are available in the assignments tab. Each session should correspond to a lecture in the above menu. A total of 4 assignments taking the form of "mini-projects" will be assigned throughout the semester. Class meets on Wednesdays at 4pm for 2h every week starting on September 23, 2026. Evaluation Criteria Continuous assessment: 50% Final project: 50% Mandatory attendance: –20% on the final grade for each unexcused absence Make-up exam ("rattrapage"): noooo pleeeaaaase :((

docs.text: Final Project Final Project The goal of the final project is to design an object based on a Teensy. It can take any form you wish: a sound or visual installation, a musical instrument (physical interface + synthesizer), a MIDI controller, etc. Your system must be placed outside the breadboard (e.g., inside a cardboard box, mounted on a mug, etc.). Feel free to make something with a "DIY" look (with tape, etc.). Projects should be carried out in groups of 2. Exceptions might be granted (talk to Romain). docs.text: Arduino Programming Basics The microcontroller used in this course is the Teensy 4.0 . It can be programmed using the Teensyduino Environment . Install information can be found here: https://www.pjrc.com/teensy/td_download.html . The Teensy 4.0 is not an Arduino per se but works exactly the same way. Hello World The following program displays "Hello World" in the Serial Monitor every 0.5 seconds. The Serial Monitor can be opened by clicking on the "magnifying glass" icon in the top right corner of the interface. void setup() { Serial.begin(9600); } void loop() { Serial.println("Hello World"); delay(500); } Counter int cnt = 0; void setup() { Serial.begin(9600); } void loop() { Serial.println(cnt); cnt = cnt+1; delay(500); } Counter up to 20 Version using the modulo ( % ) operation: int cnt = 0; void setup() { Serial.begin(9600); } void loop() { Serial.print("Counter: "); Serial.println(cnt); cnt = (cnt+1)%20; delay(500); } Version using a condition ( if ): int cnt = 0; void setup() { Serial.begin(9600); } void loop() { Serial.print("Counter: "); Serial.println(cnt); cnt = (cnt+1); if(cnt == 10){ cnt = 0; } delay(500); }

docs.text: Serial and MIDI Communication Serial Control of a Processing Program with a Teensy In this section, we show how to control a Processing program ( https://processing.org/ ) with a Teensy. What's Serial? Serial is a way of transmitting digital data "bits by bits." In that regard, it is one of the most basic digital communication protocol. The Arduino serial protocol uses 8 bits words. Arduino Program int val = 0; void setup(){ Serial.begin(9600); } void loop(){ Serial.println(val); val = (val + 1)%255; delay(10); } Processing Program import processing.serial.*; Serial myPort; static String val; int sensorVal = 0; void setup() { fullScreen(P3D); noStroke(); fill(204); String portName = "/dev/ttyACM0"; myPort = new Serial(this, portName, 9600); } void draw() { if ( myPort.available() > 0) { val = myPort.readStringUntil('\n'); try { sensorVal = Integer.valueOf(val.trim()); } catch(Exception e) { ; } } background(0); float recWidth = width/4*sensorVal/255; fill(255,0,0); square(width/2-recWidth/2, height/2-recWidth/2, recWidth); } MIDI Control With the Teensy This example shows how to use a Teensy to control a Faust program using USB MIDI. What's MIDI? MIDI is an 8 bits communication protocol used in the context of music. It dates back from 1983 and it is still in use nowadays! MIDI was designed to transmit note numbers, velocity but also generic information through control changes. More information on MIDI can be found on Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MIDI Teensy Program Choose Tools/USB Type/MIDI . void setup() { } void loop() { usbMIDI.sendControlChange(0,random(0,127),0); delay(100); } Faust Program Choose the Teensy as a MIDI input in the Faust IDE. import("stdfaust.lib"); f = hslider("freq[midi: ctrl 0]",440,50,2000,0.01) : si.smoo; process = os.sawtooth(f)*0.9;

docs.text: Basic Electronics and Analog Sensors The Teensy 4.0 Technical information and the connection layout for the Teensy 4.0 can be found on PJRC’s website: https://www.pjrc.com/store/teensy40.html Introduction to Electronics The following page: https://ccrma.stanford.edu/wiki/Introduction_to_Electronics_(condensed) provides a good overview of basic electronics concepts for building interfaces. It is highly recommended reading :). Using a Potentiometer or a Button with the Teensy The following circuit: allows you to connect a potentiometer and a button to a Teensy. Here's the corresponding picture: The values from these different elements can be displayed in the serial debugger as follows: void setup(){ pinMode(0,INPUT); Serial.begin(9600); } void loop(){ int potVal = analogRead(A0); if(digitalRead(0)){ Serial.println("On :)"); } else{ Serial.println("Off :("); } Serial.print("Pot Val: "); Serial.println(potVal); delay(100); } Exercise Mapping Printed Values Modify the range of the potentiometer so that printed values are between 300 and 400 instead of 0 and 1023. When pressing the button, values should be between 400 and 500. Possible Solution void setup(){ pinMode(0,INPUT); Serial.begin(9600); } void loop(){ int offset = 0; if(digitalRead(0)){ offset = 100; } int potVal = analogRead(A0)/1023*100 + 300 + offset; Serial.print("Pot Val: "); Serial.println(potVal); delay(100); } Implementing a Switch Modify the code from the first assignment so that switching to a new note happens when pressing the button instead of every n milliseconds. New notes should be selected once at a time: pressing the button once triggers only one new note. Possible Solution int state = HIGH; // the current state of the output pin int reading; // the current reading from the input pin int previous = LOW; // the previous reading from the input pin // the follow variables are long's because the time, measured in miliseconds, // will quickly become a bigger number than can be stored in an int. unsigned long t = 0; // the last time the output pin was toggled unsigned long debounce = 200UL; // the debounce time, increase if the output flickers char *notes[] = {"Do","Re","Mi","Fa","Sol","La","Si"}; void setup() { pinMode(0,INPUT); Serial.begin(9600); } void loop() { reading = digitalRead(0); // if the input just went from LOW and HIGH and we've waited long enough // to ignore any noise on the circuit, toggle the output pin and remember // the time if (reading == HIGH && previous == LOW && millis() - t > debounce) { if (state == HIGH) state = LOW; else{ state = HIGH; Serial.println(notes[random(7)]); } t = millis(); } previous = reading; }

docs.text: Mapping, FIltering, and Buying Stuff Mapping Techniques Sometimes the signal produced by a sensor does not span the entire range of the Arduino/Teensy analog input. For example, the values obtained may be between 234 and 769 instead of 0 and 1023. In this case, the range can be corrected using a cross-multiplication: int sensorValue = analogRead(A0); int scaledValue = (sensorValue - 234)*1023/(769-234); In practice, it is rare in this kind of situation for the minimum and maximum sensor values to be stable (e.g., the minimum value may fluctuate between 225 and 240 in the previous example). In this case, the sensor range can be "tightened" and clipped using the min and max functions: int sensorValue = analogRead(A0); int scaledValue = max(0,min(1024,(sensorValue - 245)*1023/(760-245))); Filtering It is sometimes necessary to filter values produced by some sensors to stabilize them. These filtering operations can be carried out directly on the target platform (e.g., in Faust using the si.smoo or si.smooth functions). This type of operation can be performed directly on the Arduino using a "normalized integrator" type filter: y(n) = (1-a_{1})x(n) + a_{1}y(n-1) where a_{1} is the pole of the filter (a value of 0.99 is recommended). Where to Buy Electronic Components and Materials? If you’re in a hurry, want a very large (too large) selection, flawless customer service, and don’t mind paying a bit more: https://fr.farnell.com/ If you want the essentials and are looking for pre-assembled boards: https://www.mouser.fr/ or https://www.digikey.fr If you want to buy in bulk and pay less with a limited selection: https://www.amazon.fr/ If you want unlimited choice, pay 4 times less, and have a 50% chance of getting a counterfeit: https://www.aliexpress.com/ For raw materials, you can go to any hardware store (in Sté, I personally prefer Leroy Merlin).

docs.text: Digital Fabrication for Musical Interfaces and Instruments Lecture at a glance Course: Physical Interaction Design @ UJM Duration: 2 hours Audience: Master’s students in music, sound, design, and creative technologies Prerequisites: Introductory ideas of digital musical instruments, physical interaction, and sensors Format: Illustrated lecture, examples, discussion, and a short design exercise Digital fabrication lets instrument makers move from a digital design to a physical object using machines such as 3D printers, laser cutters, and CNC routers. This lecture introduces the main fabrication processes and the software that connects design to production. Its focus is on making musical controllers and instruments: enclosures, buttons, brackets, wearable structures, acoustic parts, and assemblies that bring sensors and electronics into a playable form. The central idea is that fabrication is part of instrument design. Material, geometry, assembly, and surface affect how an object is held, struck, pressed, worn, repaired, and understood by a performer and audience. The class remains at an introductory level. Detailed machine operation belongs in a trained workshop with its own equipment-specific rules. Learning objectives By the end of the lecture, students should be able to: Distinguish additive, subtractive, and sheet-cutting processes, and give examples of each. Describe the main families of 3D printing and the kinds of objects each can produce. Explain the path from a CAD model to a slicer or CAM project, machine file, fabricated part, and assembled instrument. Recognize the roles of CAD, vector drawing, slicer, CAM, and machine-control software. Identify design constraints that matter for a physical musical interface, including fit, strength, assembly, ergonomics, and repair. Choose a plausible fabrication approach for a small musical controller and explain the choice. Suggested two-hour plan Time Section Format 0–8 min Opening: what does fabrication add to an instrument? Opening: what does fabrication add to an instrument? (0–8 min) Opening question What changes when a musical controller becomes a physical object? Invite students to name an object they have used to make or control sound: a keyboard, guitar pedal, phone, game controller, drum pad, wearable, or custom digital musical instrument (DMI). Ask what makes it playable: shape, size, texture, resistance, weight, spacing, grip, visible controls, feedback, or how it sits in a room. Digital fabrication helps make forms that are difficult, slow, or expensive to build by hand. It can produce a custom enclosure, a shaped grip, a mounting plate for sensors, a flexible prototype, or a set of linked parts. A printed box can hold electronics, but the instrument design also decides where a hand rests, how a button is found, how movement is constrained, and whether the performer can replace a broken part. Three roles for fabrication in this course Form: Enclosures, handles, keys, supports, wearables, and instrument bodies. Function: Mounting sensors, controlling cable paths, providing hinges or sliding parts, and setting the movement available to the performer. Experience: Weight, texture, visibility, reach, comfort, sound from the object itself, and the audience’s sense of cause and effect. Prompt Show or describe a simple controller with a microcontroller, one sensor, and a button. Ask: what would a fabricated housing improve? Possible answers include secure mounting, repeatable sensor placement, comfortable grip, protection during performance, and a more legible relationship between action and sound. 2. Three ways to shape material (8–18 min) Introduce the broad distinction between additive , subtractive , and forming or joining processes. Process family Basic idea Examples Typical musical-interface use Additive Build an object by adding material, often in layers FFF/FDM, SLA, SLS Custom enclosures, brackets, grips, complex shapes Subtractive Remove material from a larger piece of stock CNC routing, milling, laser cutting Panels, plates, slots, precise flat parts Forming / joining Shape or connect material without building the whole part through a toolpath Bending sheet, casting, fastening, gluing Flexible surfaces, assemblies, repairable instruments The machine does not remove the need for design decisions. Each process has a different relation to geometry, material, scale, finish, tolerances, and assembly. A part that is easy to print may be awkward to machine from a sheet; a laser-cut panel may be more useful as one face of a multi-part instrument than as a complete enclosure. Discussion: choose the process after the object Ask what the part needs to do before choosing a machine. A flat faceplate with labelled holes may be a good laser-cut part. A rounded ergonomic grip may be easier to print. A thick hardwood body with a smooth cavity might suit CNC routing. A hybrid instrument may combine all three with screws and off-the-shelf hardware. 3. 3D printing technologies (18–42 min) 3.1 Material extrusion: FFF / FDM Material extrusion feeds thermoplastic filament through a heated nozzle. The nozzle deposits paths layer by layer until the object is built. Fused filament fabrication (FFF) is the generic process name; fused deposition modeling (FDM) is a widely used commercial term. This is the most familiar desktop 3D-printing process for many students and makers. Common materials include PLA, PETG, ABS/ASA, and flexible TPU, each with different properties and print requirements. Useful for: enclosures, brackets, buttons, knobs, clips, grips, mounting fixtures, and quick shape prototypes. Design consequences: The part is built in layers, so strength can differ by direction. A thin arm may split more easily across its layers than along them. Overhangs may need support material or a changed orientation. Holes, slots, and thin walls need enough clearance and thickness for the printer and material. Orientation affects visible layer lines, surface finish, support marks, print time, and strength. Parts that must fit together often need a clearance test instead of assuming the CAD dimensions will fit exactly. 3.2 Vat photopolymerization: SLA, DLP, and MSLA Vat photopolymerization hardens liquid resin with light. In SLA , a laser traces the layer; DLP projects a layer image; MSLA/LCD exposes a layer through a light source and masking screen. Implementations differ, but all cure photosensitive liquid into a solid part. Useful for: fine details, small buttons or knobs, smooth surfaces, miniatures, and prototypes where surface quality matters. Design and process consequences: Parts often need supports and careful orientation. Uncured resin must be removed; washing and post-curing are commonly part of the process. Resin is a chemical material. Follow the printer and workshop requirements for handling, ventilation, protective equipment, and waste. Material properties differ from familiar thermoplastics; select a resin for the intended use rather than judging by appearance alone. 3.3 Powder bed fusion: SLS and metal processes Powder bed fusion uses thermal energy to fuse selected areas in a powder bed. Selective laser sintering (SLS) commonly produces polymer parts; metal powder-bed systems use a laser or electron beam to fuse metal powder. Useful for: complex parts, interlocking structures, and geometries that would otherwise need many supports. SLS parts can be useful for durable enclosures, brackets, or small-batch components when equipment and service are available. Design and process consequences: Unfused powder supports parts during the build, but it must be removed afterward. Surface texture and dimensional tolerances differ from FFF and resin processes. Equipment, material handling, and post-processing needs are more specialized than typical desktop printing. 3.4 Other additive processes The ISO/ASTM additive-manufacturing vocabulary groups processes into seven broad families. In addition to material extrusion, vat photopolymerization, and powder bed fusion, these include: Material jetting: deposits droplets of build material, often with curing. It can produce detailed, multi-material parts on specialized systems. Binder jetting: deposits a binder to join regions of powder; the part may require further processing. Directed energy deposition: deposits material while a focused energy source melts it, often for metal repair or large industrial parts. Sheet lamination: bonds sheets of material to build a part. These industrial processes are useful to know as a map of the field. The course’s practical emphasis is on selecting an appropriate process for a small instrument component, often FFF, resin printing, laser cutting, or CNC routing. 3.5 Choosing a printing process Question Why it matters Is the part a quick prototype or a finished component? Prototype parts can prioritize iteration; a finished part needs suitable material and finish. Does it need to flex, withstand impact, or carry a load? Material and build orientation affect mechanical behavior. Are small details or a smooth surface essential? Resin processes can capture fine details but add handling and post-processing. Is the geometry hard to support or assemble? Build process and part orientation can change the design. Can it be divided into simpler parts? A two-part enclosure may be easier to print, service, and revise. How will it connect to sensors, electronics, and a performer? Mounting, access, cable routing, and comfort are functional requirements. The “best” process depends on the role of the part, the available machine and material, workshop constraints, and how many iterations the project can support. 4. CAD and design for fabrication (42–54 min) 4.1 CAD is a design space, not just a drawing tool Computer-aided design (CAD) describes the geometry and relationships of a part. A parametric CAD model can preserve dimensions and constraints so that the design can be revised coherently. A mesh or sculpting tool may be better for organic forms. A 2D vector drawing is often the right starting point for flat profiles and laser-cut parts. Examples of software include: 3D parametric CAD: FreeCAD, Autodesk Fusion, Onshape, SolidWorks. Mesh and organic modeling: Blender, Meshmixer and similar tools. 2D vector drawing: Inkscape, Illustrator, and machine-specific laser software. Slicers: PrusaSlicer, Cura, OrcaSlicer, Bambu Studio, PreForm for compatible systems. CAM: FreeCAD Path/CAM, Fusion Manufacture, and machine-specific CAM tools. Machine preparation / control: LightBurn for supported laser systems, printer host software, or the CNC controller interface. These names are examples rather than endorsements. Some applications combine CAD, CAM, and machine preparation; others specialize in one step. Always confirm that the chosen software supports the actual machine and its file format. 4.2 Design for assembly and play For a musical interface, a part must fit both its components and a human action. Before modeling, identify: component dimensions and mounting-hole locations; button, knob, sensor, connector, and display positions; cable bends, access to USB or power, and room for fasteners; wall thickness, clearances, moving parts, and how parts will be assembled; reach, grip, posture, tactile feedback, and the possibility of playing without watching the control; access for repair, sensor replacement, and firmware updates. Use component datasheets and physical measurements. Add clearance for manufacturing variation and assembly. A quick test coupon or a small print of a connector opening can reveal fit problems before the full enclosure is made. Discussion: why not print the whole instrument as one part? Separate components can be easier to print, repair, and revise. A modular object can use a printed grip, a laser-cut faceplate, standard screws, a replaceable sensor mount, and a microcontroller board. Splitting the design may also improve access and reduce wasted material. 5. Short break (54–64 min) Prompt students to notice how objects around them are assembled. Which parts appear molded, printed, machined, cut from sheet, or fastened together? What design choices are visible at the joints? 6. From 3D CAD to slicer to printer (64–79 min) 6.1 The workflow CAD model → export / project file → slicer → previewed layers and toolpaths → printer-specific machine file → fabrication → support removal / finishing → assembly → test with performer → revise CAD The CAD model describes the object. The slicer prepares that model for a specific printer and material. It turns the geometry into successive layers, perimeters, infill, supports, and movement instructions. Depending on the machine, the output may be G-code or a manufacturer-specific job file. 6.2 Typical file handoff STL: common mesh format for a single surface model. It does not preserve the original parametric design history. 3MF: a 3D-printing project format that can carry model and print-plate information; useful when the slicer supports it. STEP: a solid-model exchange format often used when moving editable geometry between CAD and CAM tools. The right export depends on the next application. Check units and scale after import. A model that appears tiny or enormous may have a unit mismatch. 6.3 What the slicer controls Orientation: affects strength, surface finish, supports, and time. Layer height: affects vertical detail and build time. Perimeters and wall thickness: influence durability and the quality of screw holes or enclosures. Infill: supports upper surfaces and can alter weight and stiffness; it does not replace adequate walls where the part needs strength. Supports and adhesion aids: help difficult geometry stay attached during the print; they also need removal. Material profile: temperature, cooling, speed, and other settings depend on the printer and material. Students do not need to memorize settings at this stage. They should understand that slicing is a manufacturing decision. The same CAD model can produce different parts when orientation, material, walls, supports, or printer profile change. 6.4 Inspect before printing Use the slicer’s preview to inspect the actual planned layers and paths. Look for unsupported regions, missing walls, unexpected gaps, poor bed contact, support structures inside inaccessible cavities, and a likely weak orientation. Confirm the part fits within the machine volume and that the selected printer and material profile are correct. 6.5 After printing Remove supports and clean the part as appropriate for the process. Check the fit of controls, boards, and fasteners. Assemble the instrument, then test it with the intended gesture. Note what feels wrong: a sharp edge, a loose knob, a hidden connector, a sensor that moves, or a grip that forces an awkward posture. Return those observations to the CAD model for the next version. 7. CNC routing and CAM (79–94 min) 7.1 What a CNC router does A CNC router uses a rotating cutting tool to remove material from a workpiece. It is particularly useful for sheet goods and larger parts in wood, plastics, and some other machine-compatible materials. Many router projects are 2D or 2.5D : the tool cuts profiles, slots, pockets, and shallow shapes at different depths while the workpiece stays in one orientation. Musical-interface uses: a wooden instrument body, a faceplate, a recessed control surface, a cavity for electronics, a large mounting plate, or a repeatable set of parts. 7.2 Design consequences A round tool cannot make a perfectly sharp internal corner. Internal corners need a radius or a dog-bone relief if a square component must fit. Narrow slots and small features are limited by tool diameter and reach. The workpiece must be held securely. Workholding affects what areas the cutter can reach. Cut depth, tool choice, stock thickness, and setup affect the result. Parts may need tabs or another holding strategy so that the final cut does not release them unexpectedly. 7.3 CAD-to-CAM workflow CAD solid → CAM setup (machine, stock, origin, tool) → toolpaths → simulation and review → postprocessor → machine-specific NC / G-code → router and workholding → deburr / finish → assemble and test In CAM, the operator defines the stock, work coordinate system (WCS), tool, operations, and cutting strategy. The software generates and simulates toolpaths. A postprocessor translates those paths into code suited to the particular machine and controller. G-code is not automatically interchangeable between CNC machines. Simulation helps identify unreachable features, collisions, and incorrect setups. It does not replace checking the real stock, tool, workholding, machine limits, and workshop procedure. 7.4 Software examples FreeCAD Path/CAM and Autodesk Fusion Manufacture are examples of tools that connect solid models to CAM setup, toolpaths, simulation, and machine-specific post-processing. A simple router may instead use a more specialized 2D CAM package. Choose the postprocessor for the actual machine and verify the output through the approved workflow. 8. Laser cutting and other sheet processes (94–108 min) 8.1 Laser cutting A laser cutter follows a path across sheet material. Vector paths can be used for cuts or line marking; filled areas or raster images can be used for engraving. The software assigns operations and settings to groups or layers. For example, a design might engrave labels, score fold lines, and cut the outer profile in a planned order. Musical-interface uses: faceplates, labels, stencils, acrylic or plywood panels, finger guides, flat enclosures, and layered assemblies. Design considerations: A laser cuts 2D profiles from sheet stock; a three-dimensional object usually needs tabs, slots, spacers, bending, or fasteners. The kerf removes material along the cut. Tight-fitting parts need the kerf and material thickness accounted for. Lines that overlap can be cut more than once; inspect duplicates and closed paths. Engraving and cutting are different operations and are commonly ordered so that internal details are marked before the part is released from the sheet. Material compatibility, extraction, fire prevention, and supervision are machine- and workshop-specific. Confirm that the material is approved for the machine and follow local safety rules; do not infer safety from a material’s appearance. 8.2 Typical laser workflow 2D vector drawing → vector cleanup and scale check → operation layers → machine/material settings → preview and test piece → cut / engrave → assemble layers → fit electronics and test the interface LightBurn is one example of software that organizes vector and image work into operation layers for compatible laser systems. Inkscape and other vector editors can create the underlying 2D geometry. Some machines instead use their own software and file conventions. 8.3 Other useful digital fabrication processes Vinyl cutting: cuts thin adhesive vinyl or similar sheet materials. Useful for labels, masks, overlays, and decorative or tactile markings, rather than structural parts. Waterjet cutting: uses a high-pressure water stream, often with abrasive, to cut sheet or plate materials on specialized equipment. Digital embroidery: converts vector-like patterns into stitch instructions; useful for conductive textiles and wearable interfaces. PCB milling and fabrication: produces circuit-board prototypes through specialized processes, but the design and electrical rules require a separate lesson. Hand tools and conventional workshop processes: sanding, drilling, bending, fastening, and finishing often complete a digitally fabricated object. 8.4 Hybrid construction Different processes can complement one another. A small DMI might use a 3D-printed grip and sensor mount, a laser-cut faceplate, an off-the-shelf microcontroller, and standard screws. The choice should follow function: a fastener should remain accessible, a sensor should stay in place, and the assembled object should support the intended movement. 9. Design exercise: fabricate a musical controller (108–116 min) Brief Design a handheld sound controller with: one continuous control (for example, a knob, pressure surface, or bending gesture); one discrete control (for example, a button or switch); an accessible connection to a microcontroller and a cable or battery; a clear way for the performer to understand and repeat the gesture. Group task In five minutes, sketch the object and its fabrication plan. In three minutes, each group gives a short report. Include: The performer’s action and how the object is held or placed. The component layout: sensor, button, microcontroller, connector, and cable path. The proposed process for each major part: print, laser cut, CNC route, or buy/assemble. The software path and file handoff: CAD, vector drawing, slicer, CAM, and/or machine-control software. One likely fit, strength, comfort, or repair issue, and a way to test it. Encourage a hybrid plan. Students do not need to model the object in software; the objective is to connect the physical interaction to a plausible fabrication sequence. Debrief questions Which part sets the performer’s posture or grip? Which dimensions should be measured before modeling? What needs to remain accessible for assembly or repair? What is the first cheap prototype that could test the most important uncertainty? Which process choice depends on workshop access or safety training? 10. Summary and exit question (116–120 min) Key ideas Additive, subtractive, and sheet-based processes shape material in different ways. 3D printing is a family of technologies, not a single process. CAD describes the object; slicers and CAM tools prepare it for a specific machine and process. Machine files depend on the machine, material, process, and setup. A file that works for one machine may not suit another. Fabrication choices affect how an instrument is assembled, held, played, repaired, and perceived. A quick prototype should answer a question. It can test fit, reach, strength, balance, or gesture before the full object is made. Exit question Choose one part of a musical instrument you would fabricate. Which process would you use, what software would prepare the job, and what would you test first? Software and references Software names below are examples. Current machine compatibility, licensing, formats, and interfaces should be checked before a project begins. ISO/ASTM 52900: Additive manufacturing vocabulary NIST: Additive Manufacturing Technologies Prusa Knowledge Base: First print with PrusaSlicer Autodesk Fusion: Manufacture overview Autodesk Fusion: Setups for manufacturing LightBurn: Colors and layers Harvard Environmental Health & Safety: Laser cutter pre-use checklist Instructor note on machine safety This lecture explains process concepts and file workflows; it is not machine-operation training. Laser cutters, CNC routers, resin printers, and other fabrication equipment have different hazards and operating requirements. Students should use machines only after the relevant local training, with approved materials and machine-specific procedures. For laser work, material approval, functioning extraction, supervision, and fire precautions are essential workshop controls. For machining, follow the shop’s rules for enclosure, workholding, dust or fume control, tools, and emergency stops.

docs.text: Separate components can be easier to print, repair, and revise. A modular object can use a printed grip, a laser-cut faceplate, standard screws, a replaceable sensor mount, and a microcontroller board. Splitting the design may also improve access and reduce wasted material.
docs.title: Discussion: why not print the whole instrument as one part?

docs.text: Prompt students to notice how objects around them are assembled. Which parts appear molded, printed, machined, cut from sheet, or fastened together? What design choices are visible at the joints?
docs.title: 5. Short break (54–64 min)
6. From 3D CAD to slicer to printer (64–79 min)

docs.text: CAD model → export / project file → slicer → previewed layers and toolpaths → printer-specific machine file → fabrication → support removal / finishing → assembly → test with performer → revise CAD The CAD model describes the object. The slicer prepares that model for a specific printer and material. It turns the geometry into successive layers, perimeters, infill, supports, and movement instructions. Depending on the machine, the output may be G-code or a manufacturer-specific job file.
docs.title: 6.1 The workflow

docs.text: STL: common mesh format for a single surface model. It does not preserve the original parametric design history. 3MF: a 3D-printing project format that can carry model and print-plate information; useful when the slicer supports it. STEP: a solid-model exchange format often used when moving editable geometry between CAD and CAM tools. The right export depends on the next application. Check units and scale after import. A model that appears tiny or enormous may have a unit mismatch.
docs.title: 6.2 Typical file handoff

docs.text: Orientation: affects strength, surface finish, supports, and time. Layer height: affects vertical detail and build time. Perimeters and wall thickness: influence durability and the quality of screw holes or enclosures. Infill: supports upper surfaces and can alter weight and stiffness; it does not replace adequate walls where the part needs strength. Supports and adhesion aids: help difficult geometry stay attached during the print; they also need removal. Material profile: temperature, cooling, speed, and other settings depend on the printer and material. Students do not need to memorize settings at this stage. They should understand that slicing is a manufacturing decision. The same CAD model can produce different parts when orientation, material, walls, supports, or printer profile change.
docs.title: 6.3 What the slicer controls

docs.text: Use the slicer’s preview to inspect the actual planned layers and paths. Look for unsupported regions, missing walls, unexpected gaps, poor bed contact, support structures inside inaccessible cavities, and a likely weak orientation. Confirm the part fits within the machine volume and that the selected printer and material profile are correct.
docs.title: 6.4 Inspect before printing

docs.text: Remove supports and clean the part as appropriate for the process. Check the fit of controls, boards, and fasteners. Assemble the instrument, then test it with the intended gesture. Note what feels wrong: a sharp edge, a loose knob, a hidden connector, a sensor that moves, or a grip that forces an awkward posture. Return those observations to the CAD model for the next version.
docs.title: 6.5 After printing

docs.text: A CNC router uses a rotating cutting tool to remove material from a workpiece. It is particularly useful for sheet goods and larger parts in wood, plastics, and some other machine-compatible materials. Many router projects are 2D or 2.5D : the tool cuts profiles, slots, pockets, and shallow shapes at different depths while the workpiece stays in one orientation. Musical-interface uses: a wooden instrument body, a faceplate, a recessed control surface, a cavity for electronics, a large mounting plate, or a repeatable set of parts.
docs.title: 7.1 What a CNC router does

docs.text: A round tool cannot make a perfectly sharp internal corner. Internal corners need a radius or a dog-bone relief if a square component must fit. Narrow slots and small features are limited by tool diameter and reach. The workpiece must be held securely. Workholding affects what areas the cutter can reach. Cut depth, tool choice, stock thickness, and setup affect the result. Parts may need tabs or another holding strategy so that the final cut does not release them unexpectedly.
docs.title: 7.2 Design consequences

docs.text: CAD solid → CAM setup (machine, stock, origin, tool) → toolpaths → simulation and review → postprocessor → machine-specific NC / G-code → router and workholding → deburr / finish → assemble and test In CAM, the operator defines the stock, work coordinate system (WCS), tool, operations, and cutting strategy. The software generates and simulates toolpaths. A postprocessor translates those paths into code suited to the particular machine and controller. G-code is not automatically interchangeable between CNC machines. Simulation helps identify unreachable features, collisions, and incorrect setups. It does not replace checking the real stock, tool, workholding, machine limits, and workshop procedure.
docs.title: 7.3 CAD-to-CAM workflow

docs.text: FreeCAD Path/CAM and Autodesk Fusion Manufacture are examples of tools that connect solid models to CAM setup, toolpaths, simulation, and machine-specific post-processing. A simple router may instead use a more specialized 2D CAM package. Choose the postprocessor for the actual machine and verify the output through the approved workflow.
docs.title: 7.4 Software examples
8. Laser cutting and other sheet processes (94–108 min)

docs.text: A laser cutter follows a path across sheet material. Vector paths can be used for cuts or line marking; filled areas or raster images can be used for engraving. The software assigns operations and settings to groups or layers. For example, a design might engrave labels, score fold lines, and cut the outer profile in a planned order. Musical-interface uses: faceplates, labels, stencils, acrylic or plywood panels, finger guides, flat enclosures, and layered assemblies. Design considerations: A laser cuts 2D profiles from sheet stock; a three-dimensional object usually needs tabs, slots, spacers, bending, or fasteners. The kerf removes material along the cut. Tight-fitting parts need the kerf and material thickness accounted for. Lines that overlap can be cut more than once; inspect duplicates and closed paths. Engraving and cutting are different operations and are commonly ordered so that internal details are marked before the part is released from the sheet. Material compatibility, extraction, fire prevention, and supervision are machine- and workshop-specific. Confirm that the material is approved for the machine and follow local safety rules; do not infer safety from a material’s appearance.
docs.title: 8.1 Laser cutting

docs.text: 2D vector drawing → vector cleanup and scale check → operation layers → machine/material settings → preview and test piece → cut / engrave → assemble layers → fit electronics and test the interface LightBurn is one example of software that organizes vector and image work into operation layers for compatible laser systems. Inkscape and other vector editors can create the underlying 2D geometry. Some machines instead use their own software and file conventions.
docs.title: 8.2 Typical laser workflow

docs.text: Vinyl cutting: cuts thin adhesive vinyl or similar sheet materials. Useful for labels, masks, overlays, and decorative or tactile markings, rather than structural parts. Waterjet cutting: uses a high-pressure water stream, often with abrasive, to cut sheet or plate materials on specialized equipment. Digital embroidery: converts vector-like patterns into stitch instructions; useful for conductive textiles and wearable interfaces. PCB milling and fabrication: produces circuit-board prototypes through specialized processes, but the design and electrical rules require a separate lesson. Hand tools and conventional workshop processes: sanding, drilling, bending, fastening, and finishing often complete a digitally fabricated object.
docs.title: 8.3 Other useful digital fabrication processes

docs.text: Different processes can complement one another. A small DMI might use a 3D-printed grip and sensor mount, a laser-cut faceplate, an off-the-shelf microcontroller, and standard screws. The choice should follow function: a fastener should remain accessible, a sensor should stay in place, and the assembled object should support the intended movement.
docs.title: 8.4 Hybrid construction
9. Design exercise: fabricate a musical controller (108–116 min)

docs.text: Design a handheld sound controller with: one continuous control (for example, a knob, pressure surface, or bending gesture); one discrete control (for example, a button or switch); an accessible connection to a microcontroller and a cable or battery; a clear way for the performer to understand and repeat the gesture.
docs.title: Brief

docs.text: In five minutes, sketch the object and its fabrication plan. In three minutes, each group gives a short report. Include: The performer’s action and how the object is held or placed. The component layout: sensor, button, microcontroller, connector, and cable path. The proposed process for each major part: print, laser cut, CNC route, or buy/assemble. The software path and file handoff: CAD, vector drawing, slicer, CAM, and/or machine-control software. One likely fit, strength, comfort, or repair issue, and a way to test it. Encourage a hybrid plan. Students do not need to model the object in software; the objective is to connect the physical interaction to a plausible fabrication sequence.
docs.title: Group task

docs.text: Which part sets the performer’s posture or grip? Which dimensions should be measured before modeling? What needs to remain accessible for assembly or repair? What is the first cheap prototype that could test the most important uncertainty? Which process choice depends on workshop access or safety training?
docs.title: Debrief questions

docs.text: Additive, subtractive, and sheet-based processes shape material in different ways. 3D printing is a family of technologies, not a single process. CAD describes the object; slicers and CAM tools prepare it for a specific machine and process. Machine files depend on the machine, material, process, and setup. A file that works for one machine may not suit another. Fabrication choices affect how an instrument is assembled, held, played, repaired, and perceived. A quick prototype should answer a question. It can test fit, reach, strength, balance, or gesture before the full object is made.
docs.title: Key ideas

docs.text: Choose one part of a musical instrument you would fabricate. Which process would you use, what software would prepare the job, and what would you test first?
docs.title: Exit question

docs.text: This lecture explains process concepts and file workflows; it is not machine-operation training. Laser cutters, CNC routers, resin printers, and other fabrication equipment have different hazards and operating requirements. Students should use machines only after the relevant local training, with approved materials and machine-specific procedures. For laser work, material approval, functioning extraction, supervision, and fire precautions are essential workshop controls. For machining, follow the shop’s rules for enclosure, workholding, dust or fume control, tools, and emergency stops.
docs.title: Instructor note on machine safety

docs.text: Sensors and Sensor Technologies for Musical Interaction 1. Opening: what counts as sensing? (0–8 min) Opening question When does a movement become a musical control? Invite students to name examples: pressing a key, bowing a string, tilting a phone, turning a knob, moving a hand in front of a camera, blowing into a microphone, or touching a conductive surface. Ask whether all of these are “sensors.” The useful first distinction is that some actions are sensed by a dedicated component, while others are detected through a conventional musical interface or by analyzing an existing signal. A keyboard key may use a switch; a camera tracks visual change; a microphone converts pressure variation in air into an electrical signal. All provide information about a physical event, but they do so through different principles and with different relationships to the player. Working definition A sensor is a device or system that responds to a physical phenomenon and produces a signal that another system can use. The phenomenon might be pressure, motion, light, sound, temperature, magnetic field, distance, or a property of the body. A sensor’s output is not the gesture itself. It is a measurable trace from which a system may infer something useful. Quick classification prompt For each example, ask: what physical phenomenon changes, and what does the system observe? Example Physical phenomenon Possible observation Potentiometer knob Rotation Changing electrical resistance or voltage Push button Contact / force Open or closed circuit Accelerometer Linear acceleration Acceleration along one or more axes Camera Light arriving at an image sensor A changing image or tracked features Microphone Air pressure variation An electrical audio signal Emphasize that “sensor” can refer to a component, a module, or a larger sensing system. A camera plus computer-vision software, for example, is a sensing system even though the camera alone does not identify a hand gesture. 2. From physical event to musical consequence (8–18 min) Introduce the chain below. It helps students avoid treating a sensor reading as if it already had musical meaning. physical event → transduction → signal → interpretation → musical consequence press force sensor value “how hard?” louder / brighter Key terms Physical event: Something happens in the world: a surface is pressed, a body turns, a string vibrates. Transduction: A sensor converts one kind of physical change into another form, commonly an electrical signal. Signal: The changing value made available to the system. It may be continuous, discrete, or a stream of images or samples. Interpretation: The system decides what the signal means in context. Is a hand approaching? Is a pressure change intentional? Has a gesture started or ended? Musical consequence: The sound or behavior affected by the interpreted signal: triggering a note, changing timbre, moving a sound in space, or selecting a mode. The sensor is not the gesture The same sensor reading can have different meanings in different instruments. A rising accelerometer value may mean “increase brightness,” “move the sound upward,” “select the next sound,” or nothing at all. A camera may detect a hand, but it cannot determine whether the hand is performing, resting, or accidentally crossing the frame without additional design choices. Likewise, the same gesture can be sensed in different ways. A performer’s bending motion might be captured with a flex sensor, a camera, an inertial sensor attached to the body, or a distance sensor observing the limb. Each option affords a different playing posture and produces different data. Discussion: intention and ambiguity Ask students: If a performer shakes a controller, how could the system distinguish an intentional gesture from an accidental bump? If a hand is visible to a camera, what else would the system need to know before deciding what the hand is doing? Is ambiguity always a problem, or can it be musically useful? The goal is not to eliminate ambiguity at all costs. Ambiguous or unstable behavior can be part of an instrument’s character, but it should be a deliberate design choice. The performer needs to be able to learn the relationship and decide how to use it. 3. Sensor families I: contact, force, and deformation (18–43 min) These sensors detect events at or near a physical interface. They are often easy to understand because the performer can see and feel the contact that produces the signal. 3.1 Switches and buttons A switch reports a small number of states, often open/closed or on/off. A button can trigger a note, change a mode, select a sound bank, or confirm an action. Musical qualities: clear onset, strong causal relationship, easy to learn, useful for discrete events. Questions and limitations: Is the button easy to reach while playing? Does it require too much force? Can it be triggered accidentally? Does its binary behavior fit the musical idea, or is continuous control needed? Switches include familiar keys and buttons, but also magnetic reed switches, microswitches, and contacts made from conductive materials. A switch is a sensor even when it is built into a larger control such as a keyboard key. 3.2 Potentiometers and rotary controls A rotary potentiometer converts the rotation of a shaft into a changing electrical value. A slider potentiometer does the same for linear motion. They are common in knobs, faders, and simple controllers. Musical qualities: continuous value, visible position, direct manual control; especially useful for parameters such as level, cutoff, or blend. Questions and limitations: Does the control have a useful physical range? Can the performer find it without looking? Is a knob appropriate for a parameter that changes quickly? What happens when the control reaches its limit? Other rotary technologies include encoders, which report movement in steps and can often turn indefinitely. Unlike a potentiometer, an encoder may not have a physical position that corresponds to the parameter’s current value. That can be useful for selecting values or navigating menus, but it changes how the control communicates state. 3.3 Force, pressure, and touch Pressure-sensitive components respond to force or pressure. Examples include force-sensitive resistors, pressure pads, load cells, capacitive touch surfaces, and pressure sensors in air or fluid systems. Musical qualities: continuous or graded control; can link touch intensity to dynamics, brightness, articulation, or density; can support playing across a surface rather than pressing a conventional button. Questions and limitations: Is pressure measured consistently across the surface? Does the player need tactile feedback? Can the sensor distinguish a light touch from a firm press? How will the interaction work with gloves, sweat, or different hand sizes? Touch is not the same as force. A capacitive surface can detect a finger’s presence without measuring how hard it presses. A pressure sensor may measure force but may not know where on a broad surface the force occurred. Choosing between them depends on the intended musical action. 3.4 Bend, stretch, and deformation Flex sensors, stretch sensors, bend-sensitive materials, and conductive textiles change their electrical properties as they deform. They can be attached to gloves, fabric, soft objects, or flexible structures. Musical qualities: can make the body or a soft object part of the interface; can follow continuous deformation; can support unusual postures and tactile forms. Questions and limitations: Is the sensor measuring the intended movement, or also nearby movement? Does it return to the same value after repeated bending? Is it comfortable and robust when worn? How should the performer calibrate it? 3.5 Piezoelectric and vibration sensing Piezoelectric materials produce an electrical response when they are bent, struck, or vibrated. They are often used as contact microphones, impact sensors, or pickups attached to surfaces. Musical qualities: can detect taps, impacts, vibration, and onset details; can turn an object’s material resonance into part of the instrument; small and easy to attach. Questions and limitations: A piezo element is sensitive to how and where it is mounted. It may respond strongly to impacts and vibrations, but it is not automatically a precise measure of sustained force. It can pick up unwanted knocks or stage vibration. Compare: one musical intention, several sensors Suppose a performer wants to control the brightness of a sound while bending a finger. A flex sensor attached to the finger measures bending, but it affects comfort and may need calibration. A camera can observe the finger without attaching a sensor, but needs a clear view and may be affected by lighting or occlusion. An inertial sensor on the hand measures motion, but may not isolate one finger’s bend. A pressure surface could capture a related expressive action, such as squeezing, but changes the gesture itself. There is no universally best sensor. The choice changes the performer’s action, not just the data format. 4. Short break and observation prompt (43–53 min) Ask students to look around the room or at objects they have with them. Identify one object that senses something and one that actuates or changes something. What would change if the same object were used as a musical interface? Examples might include a phone touchscreen, a laptop trackpad, a game controller, a door handle, a smartwatch, or a wireless earbud. 5. Sensor families II: motion, distance, light, sound, and body signals (53–75 min) 5.1 Inertial sensors: accelerometers and gyroscopes An accelerometer measures acceleration. In practice, this can provide information about tilt relative to gravity, movement, vibration, or impacts. A gyroscope measures rotational speed. Devices often combine several axes of these sensors in a small inertial measurement unit (IMU); some also include a magnetometer, which senses magnetic field direction. Musical qualities: compact, wearable, and usable without a camera; can follow handheld objects or body parts; useful for tilt, shake, rotation, and movement intensity. Questions and limitations: The sensor measures motion, not a musical gesture category. Stillness, drift, orientation, and attachment position matter. A sensor on the wrist cannot necessarily distinguish wrist rotation from movement of the whole arm. Ask: what does an “up” direction mean if the instrument rotates? How could a performer reset or calibrate their position? Would a noisy but responsive signal be better for a particular sound than a very stable one? 5.2 Position, proximity, and distance Distance and proximity sensors detect whether something is nearby or how far away it is. Technologies include infrared, ultrasonic, optical time-of-flight, and radar sensing. They differ in range, field of view, accuracy, response, and sensitivity to environmental conditions. Musical qualities: support contact-free interaction; can make movement through space part of an instrument; useful for approach, withdrawal, and spatial control. Questions and limitations: What objects are detected? How broad is the sensing region? Can two hands be distinguished? Does the system behave differently under sunlight, in a reflective room, or with multiple performers nearby? 5.3 Cameras and computer vision A camera measures patterns of light over an image. Software can track image features, color regions, markers, body joints, hands, or objects. Depth cameras add distance information for pixels or regions in the image. Musical qualities: capture detailed movement without requiring a wearable sensor; can observe several performers or large gestures; supports visual feedback and audience-visible interaction. Questions and limitations: The camera needs a view of the performer. Lighting, background, clothing, occlusion, and camera position affect what can be detected. A system may track a body part without knowing its intention. The performer may need to adapt to a designated stage area or keep certain movements visible. Consider the difference between “the system sees the hand” and “the system understands the gesture.” The latter depends on tracking, interpretation, training examples, and the conditions in which the system is used. 5.4 Microphones and acoustic sensing A microphone converts changes in air pressure into an electrical signal. It may be used to capture voice or an instrument, but also to detect claps, taps, breath, environmental events, or the acoustic response of an object. Musical qualities: sound itself can become the control signal; supports voice, breath, and acoustic gestures; can avoid adding a visible control surface. Questions and limitations: The microphone may hear the loudspeakers as well as the performer. Room acoustics, noise, distance, and feedback can influence the signal. A microphone does not automatically separate one intended sound from everything else. 5.5 Biosignals and physiological measures Some systems measure signals from the body, such as muscle activity (EMG), heart activity (ECG), or brain activity (EEG). These approaches can be compelling, but their outputs are often subtle, variable, and highly dependent on contact, placement, movement, and interpretation. Musical qualities: can explore exertion, tension, breath, or physiological change as part of performance; may support interactions where conventional movement is limited. Questions and limitations: Is the signal reliable enough for the intended performance? Is the setup comfortable and repeatable? Does the system make a defensible claim about what is being measured? A biosignal should not be treated as a transparent readout of emotion or intention. 5.6 Environmental sensors Light, temperature, humidity, air quality, and other environmental measures can influence a musical system. They may respond slowly, which can be appropriate for installations or evolving compositions but less useful for fast control gestures. Ask whether the audience or performer should be able to perceive the connection between the environment and the sound. A change in room temperature that slowly alters a soundscape may make sense in an installation; it may be a poor choice for triggering a precisely timed note. 6. From sensor to microcontroller (75–93 min) The sensing principle describes what physical quantity changes. The sensor’s electrical interface describes how that change becomes available to a microcontroller. Two sensors measuring the same thing, such as distance, may use different interfaces: one may provide an analog voltage, while another may contain its own conversion electronics and communicate digitally over I²C or SPI. physical quantity → sensing element / module → electrical signal or data protocol pressure sensor voltage / GPIO / I²C / SPI ↓ microcontroller input This is a useful bridge between choosing a sensor and programming an instrument. The connection affects what hardware is needed, how many pins are used, how quickly values can be read, and how much circuitry or software is involved. The protocol does not determine the musical meaning of the signal; interpretation and mapping come afterward. 6.1 Analog outputs and ADC inputs An analog sensor produces a continuously varying electrical quantity, commonly a voltage. A microcontroller’s analog-to-digital converter (ADC) samples that voltage and represents it as a number. A potentiometer used as a voltage divider is a familiar example: turning the shaft changes the voltage at its output, and the ADC converts that voltage into a digital value. Some sensors do not directly output a voltage. A thermistor or a force-sensitive resistor, for example, changes its resistance. It needs a suitable circuit, often a voltage divider, before its state can be read by an ADC. Other analog sensors need amplification or filtering. The sensor’s datasheet and the microcontroller’s input range determine how to connect it safely. Useful properties: simple, direct, and common for continuous controls such as potentiometers, light-dependent resistors, and many force or flex sensors. Things to check: The microcontroller’s maximum input voltage. A 5 V signal can damage a 3.3 V-only input. ADC resolution and input range. These affect how finely a voltage is represented, but do not guarantee that the sensor itself is precise or stable. Whether the signal needs conditioning, such as a divider, amplifier, or filter. How many ADC channels are available and whether the required pins are already used by other hardware. 6.2 Digital GPIO: switches and logic signals A digital input reads one of a small number of logic states, usually interpreted as LOW or HIGH. A push button or limit switch can be read this way. Many microcontrollers also provide internal pull-up or pull-down resistors so an unpressed switch has a stable default state rather than a floating input. Digital does not always mean “a sensor with a data protocol.” A simple switch can connect directly to a GPIO pin, while a digital sensor module may send structured data over I²C or SPI. A switch can also produce rapid transitions as its contacts settle, called contact bounce ; software or hardware debouncing prevents one press from being interpreted as several. Some sensors communicate through pulse timing or frequency rather than a voltage level or a multi-wire bus. An ultrasonic distance module, for example, may signal a measurement using the duration of a pulse. In that case, the microcontroller measures timing on a GPIO pin. 6.3 I²C: a shared two-wire bus I²C (Inter-Integrated Circuit) is a serial communication bus commonly used for small sensors and control chips. It uses two signal wires: SDA for data and SCL for the clock, in addition to power and ground. A controller can communicate with several devices on the same bus, typically selecting each device by its address. Useful properties: only two signal wires are needed; multiple addressed devices can share the bus; many small sensor breakout boards support it. Things to check: devices need compatible logic voltage and addresses; some boards have fixed or configurable addresses; cable length and bus speed are limited by electrical properties of the bus. I²C is common for sensors such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, magnetometers, environmental sensors, and small displays. 6.4 SPI: a clocked, higher-throughput connection SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface) is another common serial interface. A typical connection uses SCLK (clock), MOSI (controller-to-device data), MISO (device-to-controller data), and a chip-select line for each device. It often supports faster data transfer than I²C, and can be useful for sensors that produce larger or faster streams of data. Useful properties: high throughput, straightforward full-duplex transfers in common configurations, and no device-address negotiation on the bus. Things to check: it uses more signal wires, usually needs a separate chip-select line per device, and the sensor and microcontroller must agree on clock mode and maximum speed. SPI is common for fast motion sensors, displays, and memory devices. 6.5 UART and other connections UART is an asynchronous serial connection using a transmit line (TX) and receive line (RX), plus a shared ground. It is common for GPS modules, some sensor boards, and communication between a microcontroller and another device. Unlike I²C and SPI, a basic UART connection does not share a clock wire; both ends must be configured for the same data rate and format. Other interfaces include one-wire buses, CAN, and USB. These may be useful in particular systems, but the central design question remains the same: what signal does the sensor provide, and what does the microcontroller need in order to read it reliably? USB is more often used to connect a microcontroller or sensor interface to a computer than to connect a bare sensing element directly to a microcontroller pin. Interface comparison Sensor output / interface Typical example Connection idea Main advantage Main consideration Analog voltage Potentiometer, some light or force sensors Signal to ADC input Direct continuous value Voltage range, ADC channels, and possible signal conditioning Resistance change Thermistor, force-sensitive resistor Divider or conditioning circuit, then ADC Simple sensing element The element alone may not provide a readable voltage Digital GPIO Button, switch Logic input pin Simple discrete state Pull-up/down and contact bounce Pulse timing / frequency Ultrasonic range module, pulse sensor GPIO plus timer/capture Encodes timing or rate The program must measure pulse width or frequency I²C Many compact motion/environment sensors SDA + SCL bus Two signal wires; multiple addressed devices Address conflicts, bus speed, wiring and voltage compatibility SPI Faster motion sensors, displays Clock + data lines + chip select High data throughput More wires and device-specific configuration UART GPS or serial sensor module TX + RX Simple point-to-point serial data Both ends must use matching settings Keep the layers distinct For any example, ask students to identify three separate things: What physical quantity is sensed? For example, acceleration, pressure, light, or temperature. How does the sensor communicate it? Analog voltage, switch state, pulse timing, I²C, SPI, or UART. What does the musical instrument do with the reading? Trigger a sound, alter a parameter, classify a gesture, or control a spatial trajectory. These layers can vary independently. An accelerometer is a sensing technology; I²C or SPI is a way of transferring its readings. A potentiometer is a rotary control; an ADC is how a microcontroller turns its voltage into a number. A digital reading is not automatically more accurate, and a higher-resolution ADC does not by itself make a more playable instrument. Practical safety and documentation note Before connecting a sensor, check its supply voltage, output voltage, pin labels, and interface in the datasheet or module documentation. Sensor boards that look similar may require different voltages or wiring. In the course’s Teensy examples, the board’s input-voltage limits and pins already used by the audio shield matter. The electronics lecture develops the actual circuits and connection procedures. 7. Choosing a sensor: design tradeoffs (93–105 min) Present sensor selection as a design question about the interaction, rather than a shopping question about component specifications. Questions to ask before choosing What physical action should matter? Touch, pressure, rotation, vibration, movement through space, breath, or a change in the environment? What should the performer feel? Contact, resistance, weight, texture, freedom of movement, or no physical object at all? What kind of control is needed? A discrete trigger, a continuous value, a position, a direction, a gesture category, or a combination? Where is the interaction taking place? At a desk, on a stage, in a gallery, in a crowded room, or while moving around? What should the audience be able to understand? Is the causal link visible, or is hidden sensing part of the intended experience? What can go wrong in use? Occlusion, drift, accidental touches, background noise, fragile attachments, inconsistent calibration, or restricted movement? How will the performer learn and control it? Is feedback provided? Can the performer predict the result and recover from errors? A practical comparison table Sensor family What it can observe Typical interaction Common design concern Switch / button Contact state Trigger or selection Accidental activation; limited states Potentiometer / encoder Rotation or position Knob, slider, navigation Physical range and visible state Force / pressure / touch Contact, force, or finger presence Pressing, squeezing, touching Force is not the same as touch; feedback and consistency Flex / stretch Deformation Bending a wearable or soft object Comfort, durability, calibration Piezo / vibration Impact or vibration Striking, scraping, listening to an object Mounting, unwanted vibration, poor sustained-force measurement Accelerometer / gyroscope Linear and rotational motion Tilt, shake, rotation, movement Orientation, attachment, drift, ambiguity Proximity / distance Nearby object or distance Hovering, approach, spatial movement Field of view, range, environment, multiple objects Camera / depth camera Image features, body parts, distance Full-body or hand movement Visibility, lighting, occlusion, interpretation Microphone Sound pressure Voice, breath, taps, acoustic events Background sound and feedback Biosignal sensor Electrical or physiological activity Muscle or body-related control Contact quality, variability, interpretation claims Four recurring tradeoffs Contact versus freedom: A wearable or attached sensor can be close to the body, but may restrict movement or change the performer’s technique. Contact-free sensing allows freedom but may constrain the performer to a sensing area. Precision versus expressiveness: A highly stable control can be useful for accurate parameter setting. A more variable signal can create rich, responsive behavior when the performer can shape it musically. Visibility versus hidden sensing: A visible knob or gesture can help the audience understand cause and effect. Hidden sensing can create surprise, but may make the performance harder to read. Rich data versus playable control: More measured dimensions do not automatically make a better instrument. A small number of well-designed controls can be more expressive and learnable than many poorly connected measurements. Short analysis: “More data ≠ better instrument” Invite students to imagine two controllers: Controller A senses one pressure value with an obvious and repeatable connection to the sound. Controller B uses a camera to extract many body landmarks, but the relationship between movement and sound is difficult to predict. Which is more expressive? There is no universal answer. Ask what kind of music, performer, rehearsal process, and audience experience each design supports. Expression depends on the instrument’s possible actions, feedback, and learnability, not simply on the number of sensor channels. 8. An object instrument: A wooden object should produce different sounds when tapped, rubbed, squeezed, or tilted. A spatial performance: A performer wants to move a sound source around an audience without touching a controller. A breath instrument: A performer wants to shape a sustained sound with breathing while also triggering discrete events. Group task For each brief, students have 8 minutes to sketch a sensing design and 4 minutes for quick reports. Their sketch should include: the physical action to be sensed; one primary sensor family and one alternative; what the sensor actually measures; how its output could reach a microcontroller (for example, an ADC input, digital pin, I²C, or SPI); the musical parameter or event that could be controlled; one likely failure or ambiguity; a way to make the interaction learnable and playable. Encourage students to draw the performer and sensor placement, not just a block diagram. Ask them to show what the performer does, what the system detects, and what sound changes. Debrief prompts Did the chosen sensor preserve or change the performer’s gesture? What could be confused with an intentional action? What information did the group decide not to measure? How would the performer know that the system detected the action? Would the design work on stage, or only in a controlled classroom? 9. Sensor technologies differ in what they can observe and in the actions they ask of the performer. The same gesture can be sensed in many ways, and each way changes the instrument’s feel and constraints. A good sensor choice begins with the desired interaction and musical behavior. Sensor selection includes both the physical sensing principle and the electrical interface to the microcontroller. A playable instrument needs a learnable relationship between action, feedback, and sound; more data alone does not provide that relationship.
